title: Gradient-Based Program Synthesis with Neurally Interpreted Languages
one_liner: Teach a neural network to invent and refine its own programming language using gradient descent, bridging symbolic compositionality with deep learning flexibility.
lead: Program induction — teaching machines to write code — faces a hard trade-off. Symbolic methods write neat, reusable code but only work on domains they were built for. Neural methods adapt to any problem but produce spaghetti that does not compose and fails on new tasks. This paper bridges that divide: a system that learns its own discrete programming language end-to-end, discovering primitive operations and refining them at test time by nudging the program toward examples that work better.

paras: Symbolic program induction writes explicit code: a rule engine that outputs if-then statements, loops, and function calls. This code generalizes—a rule learned on one dataset ports to similar problems. But building the rule grammar is labor-intensive, and each new domain needs a fresh grammar.

Neural approaches learn directly from data: a neural network guesses the program from examples. The catch: the learned program is a black-box computation graph. When you test it on a new variant (different input size, unseen operation order), it crumbles. A neural network trained to add two 3-digit numbers fails on 4-digit addition.
A beginner might try: use a big neural network with more layers. This fails because the network memorizes training examples but does not invent the underlying rule.

callout.html: Neural Language Interpreter learns a discrete programming language automatically, then refines that language at test time by nudging primitive choices to adapt to new problems.

panels.title: 1. The problem
panels.viz_args: Symbolic: rigid grammar. Neural: black box.
panels.caption: Symbolic code is reusable but hard to build. Neural code adapts but does not generalize.

panels.title: 2. Discover primitives
panels.caption: Network finds primitive operations (add, copy, swap). Some are core, some rarely used.

panels.title: 3. Build programs
panels.caption: Combine primitives into variable-length sequences. Each sequence is a program.

panels.title: 4. Refine with nudging
panels.caption: At test time, nudge primitive choices based on error. No retraining needed.

panels.title: 5. The payoff
panels.caption: Programs compose like symbolic code. Refinement adapts like neural networks.

steps.text: The network discovers atomic operations (arithmetic, memory access, control flow) during training.
Each program is a variable-length sequence of primitives, not a fixed computation graph.

steps.b: Relax discrete choices into smooth decisions
steps.text: A mathematical relaxation trick pretends discrete primitive choices are smooth, so nudging signals can steer them.
A differentiable executor runs the primitives in sequence, producing an output.
Given a new task, nudge the program choices based on errors to fit the new data, without retraining.

paras: Instead of asking 'what weights should this network have?', NLI asks 'what sequence of discrete operations should this program run?' The paper moves the optimization target from continuous weights to discrete program sequences.

hidden.h2: The program likelihood under the learned language
hidden.name: How well each primitive fits the task
paras: Behind every program choice sits a confidence score: how likely is this primitive the right next step for this input? This score comes from the network's learned understanding of the task. When the network sees a new task at test time, these scores start misaligned. Refining them through nudging makes the program adapt.

The paper estimates this score by running the current program on examples and measuring the error (how far the program's output sits from the correct answer). Large error signals 'the program is wrong' and nudging shifts the primitive choices to reduce it.

heat.caption: Darker means higher confidence that this primitive belongs in the program.

reads.html: The network learns which operations are most useful for each type of task. At test time, if the current program fails on a new case, the network shifts its confidence toward operations that would fix the error.
NLI computes per-primitive scores via the neural executor's error flow. A relaxation technique makes these discrete choices smooth, enabling test-time nudging to refine the program.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: The core trick: ask the network to output a sequence of discrete choices (which primitive at step 1, which at step 2, etc.) instead of a long list of numbers that a neural network would have. Discrete choices seem incompatible with the standard training method (nudging the numbers to shrink error), so the paper uses a relaxation technique that pretends each discrete choice is smooth. This allows the entire program to be trained end-to-end by nudging, discovering which primitives are useful.

At test time, given a new task with examples, the network makes an initial program guess. The error on those examples (the distance between the program's output and the correct answer) points toward better primitive choices, because the paper has made the primitive choices differentiable — small shifts in those choices propagate backward to show which shifts would reduce the error. The paper nudges the program choices through the differentiable executor to refine the program — no retraining, just small adjustments to which primitives are chosen. This works well because the program can now change length (add or remove steps) and composition (use different primitives), adapting faster than a neural network locked in place after training.

Why this bridges the gap: symbolic methods gain compositionality (discrete primitives combine naturally); neural methods gain test-time flexibility (gradients adapt the program to new data). The result solves complex problems that require rapid adaptation to unseen tasks, because the program structure itself can be refined.

stages.s: Adapted program for the new task

math.words: To adapt at test time, nudge each primitive choice in the direction that reduces error, weighted by how much that choice affects the final answer.
symbols: the network's confidence in primitive i at position i
how far the program output is from the correct answer
the gradient: how much error changes when choice_i changes
the step size; how aggressively to nudge

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the program currently picks primitives [add, copy, multiply] and makes an error of 5.0 on the test example.
The gradient says: add contributes -0.2 to error change (reducing add hurts), copy contributes +0.8 (reducing copy helps), multiply contributes +0.1.
Update: add_new = add - 0.1 * (-0.2) = add + 0.02; copy_new = copy - 0.1 * 0.8 = copy - 0.08; multiply_new = multiply - 0.1 * 0.1 = multiply - 0.01.
The program now trusts copy less and add more, biasing the next run toward using copy less.

math.note: Nudging through the executor allows the program to adapt to new tasks without retraining, because the primitive choices can move independently without touching the rest of the network.

charts.title: Neural network only
charts.note: Neural networks memorize training but fail on new tasks. Retraining is slow.

charts.title: NLI with test-time adaptation
charts.note: NLI adapts rapidly because it refines the program structure, not the entire network.

items.b: Primitive vocabulary too large or small.
items.html: If the network discovers too many primitives, the program becomes cluttered and refinement is noisy. Too few, and the network cannot express the task. The paper must tune the vocabulary size per domain.
A long program sequence (many primitives chained together) can make gradients shrink to zero by the time they reach the first primitive choices. This blocks test-time refinement for complex programs.

Refining the program at test time on a handful of examples can fit too closely to those examples, learning quirks instead of the true rule. Using a gentle penalty on large changes or stopping nudging early can prevent this.
Choose primitives that decompose the problem naturally, use shallow program depths, and validate on held-out adaptation examples to catch overfitting.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a task where the training set uses inputs of one size and the test set uses a different size (e.g., adding 2-digit numbers in training, 4-digit in testing). Train NLI end-to-end on the training set. At test time, run gradient descent on the test examples to refine the program. Measure the accuracy on unseen test inputs of the new size. Compare to a frozen neural network and to in-context learning.
demo.closing: The demo must show that a few nudges on a handful of new examples move the program's accuracy noticeably higher, proving that test-time refinement is working.
